claim: In both Drosophila and mammals, the brain contains the most diverse population of cell types of any tissue.
source: In both Drosophila and mammals, the brain contains the most diverse population of cell types of any tissue.
evidence: This is a general statement about brain cellular diversity that draws from established scientific knowledge in the field.

claim: Transcriptional diversity is an early step in generating neuronal and glial diversity.
source: It is generally accepted that transcriptional diversity is an early step in generating neuronal and glial diversity, followed by the establishment of a unique gene expression profile that determines morphology, connectivity, and function.
evidence: This claim is supported by general scientific consensus in the field of developmental neuroscience.

claim: In Drosophila, there are two types of neural stem cells, called Type 1 (T1) and Type 2 (T2) neuroblasts.
source: In Drosophila, there are two types of neural stem cells, called Type 1 (T1) and Type 2 (T2) neuroblasts.
evidence: This is established knowledge about Drosophila neural stem cell types.

claim: The diversity of T2-derived neurons contributes a large portion of the central complex (CX).
source: The diversity of T2-derived neurons contributes a large portion of the central complex (CX), a conserved brain region that plays a role in sensorimotor integration.
evidence: This claim is supported by established knowledge in the field.

claim: The central complex is a conserved brain region that plays a role in sensorimotor integration.
source: The diversity of T2-derived neurons contributes a large portion of the central complex (CX), a conserved brain region that plays a role in sensorimotor integration.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the function of the central complex.

claim: Recent work has revealed much of the connectome of the CX.
source: Recent work has revealed much of the connectome of the CX, but how this connectome is assembled remains unclear.
evidence: This claim references recent scientific work in the field without specific citations in this sentence.

claim: How the central complex connectome is assembled remains unclear.
source: Recent work has revealed much of the connectome of the CX, but how this connectome is assembled remains unclear.
evidence: This identifies a gap in current knowledge.

claim: The study performed single nuclei RNA sequencing of T2 neuroblast-derived adult neurons and glia.
source: Here we perform single nuclei RNA sequencing of T2 neuroblast-derived adult neurons and glia.
evidence: This describes the experimental approach used in the study.

claim: The study identified clusters containing all known classes of glia.
source: We identify clusters containing all known classes of glia, clusters that are male/female enriched, and 161 neuron-specific clusters.
evidence: This is a finding from the snRNA-seq data analysis.

claim: The study identified clusters that are male/female enriched.
source: We identify clusters containing all known classes of glia, clusters that are male/female enriched, and 161 neuron-specific clusters.
evidence: This is a finding from the snRNA-seq data analysis.

claim: The study identified 161 neuron-specific clusters.
source: We identify clusters containing all known classes of glia, clusters that are male/female enriched, and 161 neuron-specific clusters.
evidence: This is a finding from the snRNA-seq data analysis shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The study mapped neurotransmitter and neuropeptide expression.
source: We map neurotransmitter and neuropeptide expression and identify unique transcription factor combinatorial codes for each cluster.
evidence: This describes analyses performed on the snRNA-seq data.

claim: The study identified unique transcription factor combinatorial codes for each cluster.
source: We map neurotransmitter and neuropeptide expression and identify unique transcription factor combinatorial codes for each cluster.
evidence: This is a finding from the transcription factor analysis shown in Figure 7.

claim: The study mapped several columnar neuron subtypes to distinct clusters.
source: We map several columnar neuron subtypes to distinct clusters and identify two neuronal classes (NPF+ and AstA+) that both map to two closely related clusters.
evidence: This describes mapping results shown in Figures 8 and 9.

claim: NPF+ and AstA+ neurons both map to two closely related clusters.
source: We map several columnar neuron subtypes to distinct clusters and identify two neuronal classes (NPF+ and AstA+) that both map to two closely related clusters.
evidence: This is a finding from the neuropeptide expression analysis shown in Figure 6.

claim: Each transcriptional cluster represents one or a few closely related neuron subtypes.
source: Our data support the hypothesis that each transcriptional cluster represents one or a few closely related neuron subtypes.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the data based on the mapping results.

claim: The laterally positioned optic lobes have been well characterized for transcriptionally distinct neurons and glia.
source: In Drosophila, the laterally positioned optic lobes have been well characterized for transcriptionally distinct neurons and glia (Konstantinides et al., 2018; Konstantinides et al., 2022; Özel et al., 2022), as has the central brain and ventral nerve cord (Croset et al., 2018; Davie et al., 2018; Lago-Baldaia et al., 2023; Li et al., 2022; McLaughlin et al., 2021; Naidu et al., 2020; Nguyen et al., 2021; Sato and Suzuki, 2022; Shu et al., 2023; Velten et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to previous studies.

claim: The central brain and ventral nerve cord have been well characterized for transcriptionally distinct neurons and glia.
source: In Drosophila, the laterally positioned optic lobes have been well characterized for transcriptionally distinct neurons and glia (Konstantinides et al., 2018; Konstantinides et al., 2022; Özel et al., 2022), as has the central brain and ventral nerve cord (Croset et al., 2018; Davie et al., 2018; Lago-Baldaia et al., 2023; Li et al., 2022; McLaughlin et al., 2021; Naidu et al., 2020; Nguyen et al., 2021; Sato and Suzuki, 2022; Shu et al., 2023; Velten et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to previous studies.

claim: The mushroom body is used for learning and memory.
source: The central brain contains many diverse neurons that populate important neuropils, such as the mushroom body (MB) used for learning and memory (Sgammeglia and Sprecher, 2022), or the central complex (CX) used for celestial navigation and sensory-motor integration (Fisher, 2022), among other behaviors.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Sgammeglia and Sprecher, 2022.

claim: The central complex is used for celestial navigation and sensory-motor integration.
source: The central brain contains many diverse neurons that populate important neuropils, such as the mushroom body (MB) used for learning and memory (Sgammeglia and Sprecher, 2022), or the central complex (CX) used for celestial navigation and sensory-motor integration (Fisher, 2022), among other behaviors.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Fisher, 2022.

claim: T1 NBs undergo asymmetric divisions to self-renew and generate a series of ganglion mother cells (GMCs).
source: T1 NBs undergo asymmetric divisions to self-renew and generate a series of ganglion mother cells (GMCs), which each produce two post-mitotic neurons (Pollington et al., 2023; Yu et al., 2010; Yu et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Pollington et al., 2023; Yu et al., 2010; Yu et al., 2013.

claim: Each GMC produces two post-mitotic neurons.
source: T1 NBs undergo asymmetric divisions to self-renew and generate a series of ganglion mother cells (GMCs), which each produce two post-mitotic neurons (Pollington et al., 2023; Yu et al., 2010; Yu et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Pollington et al., 2023; Yu et al., 2010; Yu et al., 2013.

claim: There are ~100 T1 NBs per larval central brain lobe.
source: There are ~100 T1 NBs per larval central brain lobe that each generate 20–100 neurons and glia (Ito et al., 2013; Yu et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Ito et al., 2013; Yu et al., 2013.

claim: Each T1 NB generates 20–100 neurons and glia.
source: There are ~100 T1 NBs per larval central brain lobe that each generate 20–100 neurons and glia (Ito et al., 2013; Yu et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Ito et al., 2013; Yu et al., 2013.

claim: Type 0 (T0) NBs generate post-mitotic neuron progeny.
source: In addition, there are Type 0 (T0) NBs which generate post-mitotic neuron progeny (Baumgardt et al., 2014); T0 NB lineages yet to be documented in the central brain.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Baumgardt et al., 2014.

claim: T0 NB lineages have yet to be documented in the central brain.
source: In addition, there are Type 0 (T0) NBs which generate post-mitotic neuron progeny (Baumgardt et al., 2014); T0 NB lineages yet to be documented in the central brain.
evidence: This identifies a gap in current knowledge.

claim: T2 NBs have a more complex division pattern than T1 NBs.
source: T2 NBs have a more complex division pattern than T1 NBs (Bello et al., 2008; Boone and Doe, 2008; Bowman et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Bello et al., 2008; Boone and Doe, 2008; Bowman et al., 2008.

claim: T2 NBs undergo asymmetric division to self-renew and generate an intermediate neural progenitor (INP).
source: T2 NBs undergo asymmetric division to self-renew and generate an intermediate neural progenitor (INP); each INP undergoes 4–6 divisions to self-renew and generate a GMC and its two neuron or glial progeny (Bello et al., 2008; Boone and Doe, 2008; Bowman et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Bello et al., 2008; Boone and Doe, 2008; Bowman et al., 2008.

claim: Each INP undergoes 4–6 divisions to self-renew and generate a GMC and its two neuron or glial progeny.
source: T2 NBs undergo asymmetric division to self-renew and generate an intermediate neural progenitor (INP); each INP undergoes 4–6 divisions to self-renew and generate a GMC and its two neuron or glial progeny (Bello et al., 2008; Boone and Doe, 2008; Bowman et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Bello et al., 2008; Boone and Doe, 2008; Bowman et al., 2008.

claim: Each T2 NB division will generate 8–12 progeny cells.
source: Thus, each T2 NB division will generate 8–12 progeny cells.
evidence: This is inferred from the division pattern described for T2 NBs and INPs.

claim: Most T2 NBs generate ~500 neurons.
source: Most T2 NBs generate ~500 neurons (Yu et al., 2013), have highly complex neuronal cell types based on morphology and connectivity (Hulse et al., 2020; Wang et al., 2014; Yang et al., 2013; Yu et al., 2013), and produce the columnar neurons of the adult CX (Boyan and Williams, 2011; Kandimalla et al., 2023).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Yu et al., 2013.

claim: T2 NBs have highly complex neuronal cell types based on morphology and connectivity.
source: Most T2 NBs generate ~500 neurons (Yu et al., 2013), have highly complex neuronal cell types based on morphology and connectivity (Hulse et al., 2020; Wang et al., 2014; Yang et al., 2013; Yu et al., 2013), and produce the columnar neurons of the adult CX (Boyan and Williams, 2011; Kandimalla et al., 2023).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Hulse et al., 2020; Wang et al., 2014; Yang et al., 2013; Yu et al., 2013.

claim: T2 NBs produce the columnar neurons of the adult CX.
source: Most T2 NBs generate ~500 neurons (Yu et al., 2013), have highly complex neuronal cell types based on morphology and connectivity (Hulse et al., 2020; Wang et al., 2014; Yang et al., 2013; Yu et al., 2013), and produce the columnar neurons of the adult CX (Boyan and Williams, 2011; Kandimalla et al., 2023).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Boyan and Williams, 2011; Kandimalla et al., 2023.

claim: Single-cell RNA-seq has been done on adult central brain neurons and glia.
source: Although single-cell RNA-seq (scRNA-seq) has been done on adult central brain neurons and glia (Croset et al., 2018), the transcriptomic profile of T1 versus T2 neuronal and glial progeny has not yet been characterized.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Croset et al., 2018.

claim: The transcriptomic profile of T1 versus T2 neuronal and glial progeny has not yet been characterized.
source: Although single-cell RNA-seq (scRNA-seq) has been done on adult central brain neurons and glia (Croset et al., 2018), the transcriptomic profile of T1 versus T2 neuronal and glial progeny has not yet been characterized.
evidence: This identifies a gap in current knowledge that the study addresses.

claim: T2 lineages generate diverse neuronal progeny.
source: Furthermore, the T2 lineages generate diverse neuronal progeny (Hulse et al., 2020; Wang et al., 2014; Yang et al., 2013; Yu et al., 2013) but focused transcriptional profiling of T2-derived progeny has not been reported.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Hulse et al., 2020; Wang et al., 2014; Yang et al., 2013; Yu et al., 2013.

claim: Focused transcriptional profiling of T2-derived progeny has not been reported.
source: Furthermore, the T2 lineages generate diverse neuronal progeny (Hulse et al., 2020; Wang et al., 2014; Yang et al., 2013; Yu et al., 2013) but focused transcriptional profiling of T2-derived progeny has not been reported.
evidence: This identifies a gap in current knowledge that the study addresses.

claim: The study generated a single nuclei atlas of T2-derived progeny of the adult central brain.
source: In this report, we generate a single nuclei (snRNA-seq) atlas of T2-derived progeny of the adult central brain.
evidence: This describes the main experimental approach of the study.

claim: The study used several complementary methods to link neuron identity to transcriptional clusters.
source: We use several complementary methods to link neuron identity to transcriptional clusters.
evidence: This describes the analytical approach shown in Figures 8 and 9.

claim: The data will facilitate linking neuronal transcriptomes with connectomes to gain a molecular understanding of CX development, connectivity, and behavior.
source: Our data will facilitate linking neuronal transcriptomes with connectomes to gain a molecular understanding of CX development, connectivity, and behavior.
evidence: This is a statement about the potential future utility of the data.

claim: The adult central brain is composed of neuronal and glial progeny derived from both T1 and T2 NBs.
source: The adult central brain (i.e. brain without optic lobes) is composed of neuronal and glial progeny derived from both T1 and T2 NBs.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the composition of the central brain.

claim: The study generated a transcriptomic atlas of all central brain neurons derived from both T1 and T2 NBs.
source: We first generated a transcriptomic atlas of all central brain neurons derived from both T1 and T2 NBs.
evidence: This describes the experimental approach shown in Figure 1.

claim: The study sequenced a total of 30,699 nuclei at 589 median genes per nuclei from the T1+T2 central brain.
source: We sequenced a total of 30,699 nuclei at 589 median genes per nuclei from the T1+T2 central brain.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the sequencing experiment.

claim: The study assigned 3,125 nuclei as being derived from T2 lineages based on expression of RFP, GFP, or FLP.
source: We assigned 3,125 nuclei which have expression of RFP, GFP, or FLP as being derived from T2 lineages.
evidence: This describes the method for identifying T2-derived nuclei.

claim: The study assigned 27,574 triple-negative nuclei as derived from the T1 lineages.
source: We assigned 27,574 triple-negative nuclei as derived from the T1 lineages.
evidence: This describes the method for identifying T1-derived nuclei.

claim: The study used Seurat for filtering, integrating, and clustering the atlas.
source: We used Seurat for filtering, integrating, and clustering the atlas to provide transcriptionally unique cell clusters (Stuart et al., 2019).
evidence: This describes the computational method used, supported by citation to Stuart et al., 2019.

claim: The study used UMAP-based dimension reduction to visualize the 152 clusters.
source: We used uniform manifold approximation and projection (UMAP)-based dimension reduction to visualize the 152 clusters (Figure 1B).
evidence: This describes the visualization method used, shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The T1+T2 atlas contains 152 clusters.
source: We used uniform manifold approximation and projection (UMAP)-based dimension reduction to visualize the 152 clusters (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the clustering analysis shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The study used known markers to identify distinct cell types in the central brain.
source: We used known markers (Supplementary file 2; Croset et al., 2018; Davie et al., 2018) to identify distinct cell types in the central brain, including glia, mushroom body neurons, olfactory projection neurons, clock neurons, Poxn+ neurons, serotonergic neurons, dopaminergic neurons, octopaminergic neurons, corazonergic neurons, hemocytes, and ocelli (Figure 1B; Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This describes the method for cell type identification, supported by citations and shown in Figure 1B.

claim: No cluster exclusively contained progeny from T1 or T2 NB lineages.
source: We did not observe any cluster exclusively containing progeny from T1 or T2 NB lineages (Figure 1C, Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a finding from the analysis shown in Figure 1C and Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Both T1 and T2 generate transcriptionally similar cells, despite their different developmental origins.
source: We conclude that both T1 and T2 generate transcriptionally similar cells, despite their different developmental origins.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the finding that no cluster exclusively contains T1 or T2 progeny.

claim: Deeper sequencing may resolve a single cluster into two clusters with each derived from T1 or T2 lineages.
source: Alternatively, deeper sequencing may resolve a single cluster into two clusters with each derived from T1 or T2 lineages.
evidence: This is a speculative alternative explanation for the mixed lineage clusters.

claim: T2 enriched clusters show high expression of AstA, SerT, Tk, and Vmat.
source: We next searched for cluster-defining genes in the T2 enriched clusters (Figure 1C') and found high expression of AstA (Allatostatin A), SerT (Serotonin transporter), Tk (Tachykinin), and Vmat (Vesicular monoamine transporter) (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is a finding from the gene expression analysis shown in Figure 1D.

claim: AstA+ neurons, serotonergic neurons, and TK+ neurons may be primarily derived from T2 lineages.
source: These enriched marker genes suggest that AstA+ neurons, serotonergic neurons, and TK+ neurons may be primarily derived from T2 lineages.
evidence: This is an inference based on the enrichment of specific markers in T2 clusters.

claim: The study identified 3409 glial nuclei from clusters that expressed the pan-glial marker repo in the T1+T2 atlas.
source: We focused on the 3409 glial nuclei from clusters that expressed the pan-glial marker repo (Campbell et al., 1994; Xiong et al., 1994) in the T1+T2 atlas (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the glial analysis shown in Figure 1E, supported by citations.

claim: Each glial cluster contained a mix of T1 and T2 glial progeny.
source: Each cluster contained a mix of T1 and T2 glial progeny (Figure 1E').
evidence: This is a finding from the glial analysis shown in Figure 1E'.

claim: The study identified six known glial cell types: astrocytes, cortex, ensheathing, surface glial and the two subtypes: perineurial and subperineurial.
source: We identified six known glial cell types (astrocytes, cortex, ensheathing, surface glial and the two subtypes: perineurial and subperineurial) based on canonical glial makers (Figure 1F; Supplementary file 3).
evidence: This is a finding from the glial analysis shown in Figure 1F.

claim: Some glial subtypes (astrocytes, ensheathing, and subperineurial) map to multiple clusters.
source: Similar to a previous glial cell atlas (Lago-Baldaia et al., 2023), we found some glial subtypes (astrocytes, ensheathing, and subperineurial) mapping to multiple clusters (Figure 1E and F).
evidence: This is a finding from the glial analysis shown in Figure 1E and F, compared to a previous study.

claim: A glial cluster expressed genes associated with extracellular matrix, vkg and Col4a1.
source: We identified a glial cluster that expressed genes associated with extracellular matrix, vkg and Col4a1 (Figure 1F), which have previously been identified as pan surface glial markers (DeSalvo et al., 2014; Hindle and Bainton, 2014).
evidence: This is a finding from the glial analysis shown in Figure 1F, supported by citations.

claim: The two surface glial subtypes, perineurial and subperineurial clusters, do not express vkg and Col4a1 at cluster defining levels.
source: Interestingly, the two surface glial subtypes, perineurial and subperineurial clusters, do not express these markers at cluster defining levels, and conversely the surface glia cluster 5 does not express perineurial or subperineurial specific makers (Figure 1F, Supplementary file 4).
evidence: This is a finding from the glial marker analysis shown in Figure 1F.

claim: Surface glia cluster 5 does not express perineurial or subperineurial specific markers.
source: Interestingly, the two surface glial subtypes, perineurial and subperineurial clusters, do not express these markers at cluster defining levels, and conversely the surface glia cluster 5 does not express perineurial or subperineurial specific makers (Figure 1F, Supplementary file 4).
evidence: This is a finding from the glial marker analysis shown in Figure 1F.

claim: Differential gene expression analysis for all genes between T1 and T2 glial progeny did not show differences across any glial cell types or clusters.
source: Differential gene expression analysis for all genes between T1 and T2 glial progeny did not show differences across any glial cell types or clusters (Supplementary file 5).
evidence: This is a finding from the differential expression analysis.

claim: The adult central brain contains known glial cell types with no differences in gene expression between T1 and T2-derived glia.
source: We conclude that the adult central brain contains known glial cell types with no differences in gene expression between T1 and T2-derived glia.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the differential expression analysis.

claim: The study generated a T1 neuron atlas containing 22,807 T1-derived neurons that form 114 clusters.
source: We then generated a T1 neuron atlas containing 22,807 T1-derived neurons that form 114 clusters.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the T1 neuron analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: The T1 atlas contains the expected abundance of neuronal diversity seen in previous scRNA-seq atlases.
source: We conclude that our T1-derived nuclei contain the expected abundance of neuronal diversity seen in previous scRNA-seq atlases (Croset et al., 2018; Davie et al., 2018; Li et al., 2022).
evidence: This is a conclusion based on comparison with previous studies.

claim: T2-derived cells represent a minor contribution to the whole brain atlas due to their low nuclei numbers relative to the T1-derived neurons.
source: In our whole brain atlas described above, T2-derived cells represent a minor contribution to the atlas due to their low nuclei numbers relative to the T1-derived neurons (Raji and Potter, 2021).
evidence: This is an observation about the composition of the atlas, supported by a citation.

claim: The study used FACS to select nuclei labeled by T2-specific permanent lineage tracing.
source: We used fluorescence-activated cell sorting (FACS) to select nuclei that are labeled by T2-specific permanent lineage tracing (Figure 1A and B).
evidence: This describes the experimental method used to enrich for T2 nuclei.

claim: The study sequenced 61,118 T2 nuclei.
source: In total, we sequenced 61,118 T2 nuclei.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the T2 sequencing experiment.

claim: The study included 3125 UAS transgene-labeled nuclei from the dissociated central brain without sorting from the T1+T2 atlas.
source: We included 3125 UAS transgene-labeled nuclei from the dissociated central brain without sorting from the T1+T2 atlas (see above).
evidence: This describes the composition of the T2 atlas dataset.

claim: The study generated an atlas containing 64,243 nuclei that formed 198 clusters.
source: We used integration in Seurat to generate an atlas containing 64,243 nuclei that formed 198 clusters.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the integrated T2 atlas.

claim: T2 NBs have been estimated to produce ~5000 neurons/glia in the central brain.
source: T2 NBs have been estimated to produced ~5000 neurons/glia in the central brain (Ito et al., 2013; Yang et al., 2013), with ~1800 neurons in the central complex (Hulse et al., 2020; Schlegel et al., 2024), giving our atlas ~12 x coverage.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Ito et al., 2013; Yang et al., 2013.

claim: T2 NBs produce ~1800 neurons in the central complex.
source: T2 NBs have been estimated to produced ~5000 neurons/glia in the central brain (Ito et al., 2013; Yang et al., 2013), with ~1800 neurons in the central complex (Hulse et al., 2020; Schlegel et al., 2024), giving our atlas ~12 x coverage.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Hulse et al., 2020; Schlegel et al., 2024.

claim: The T2 atlas has ~12 x coverage of T2-derived neurons.
source: T2 NBs have been estimated to produced ~5000 neurons/glia in the central brain (Ito et al., 2013; Yang et al., 2013), with ~1800 neurons in the central complex (Hulse et al., 2020; Schlegel et al., 2024), giving our atlas ~12 x coverage.
evidence: This is calculated from the number of sequenced nuclei relative to the estimated total number of T2-derived neurons.

claim: The T2 neuron cell atlas contains 50,148 non-glial nuclei forming 161 clusters.
source: We next filtered out the repo+ glial cell clusters to generate a T2 neuron cell atlas with 50,148 non-glial nuclei forming 161 clusters (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the T2 neuron atlas shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Each cluster within the T2 neuron atlas represents a transcriptionally unique cell type.
source: We conclude that each cluster within our T2 neuron atlas represents a transcriptionally unique cell type.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the cluster marker analysis shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Cholinergic neurons were most abundant (21%) in T2-derived neurons.
source: In neurons, we found that cholinergic neurons were most abundant (21%), followed by glutamatergic neurons (12%), GABAergic neurons (9%), tyraminergic neurons (2.6%), dopaminergic neurons (1.2%), serotonergic neurons (1.2%), and octopaminergic neurons (0.7%).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the neurotransmitter expression analysis shown in Figure 3.

claim: Glutamatergic neurons comprise 12% of T2-derived neurons.
source: In neurons, we found that cholinergic neurons were most abundant (21%), followed by glutamatergic neurons (12%), GABAergic neurons (9%), tyraminergic neurons (2.6%), dopaminergic neurons (1.2%), serotonergic neurons (1.2%), and octopaminergic neurons (0.7%).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the neurotransmitter expression analysis shown in Figure 3.

claim: GABAergic neurons comprise 9% of T2-derived neurons.
source: In neurons, we found that cholinergic neurons were most abundant (21%), followed by glutamatergic neurons (12%), GABAergic neurons (9%), tyraminergic neurons (2.6%), dopaminergic neurons (1.2%), serotonergic neurons (1.2%), and octopaminergic neurons (0.7%).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the neurotransmitter expression analysis shown in Figure 3.

claim: Tyraminergic neurons comprise 2.6% of T2-derived neurons.
source: In neurons, we found that cholinergic neurons were most abundant (21%), followed by glutamatergic neurons (12%), GABAergic neurons (9%), tyraminergic neurons (2.6%), dopaminergic neurons (1.2%), serotonergic neurons (1.2%), and octopaminergic neurons (0.7%).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the neurotransmitter expression analysis shown in Figure 3.

claim: Dopaminergic neurons comprise 1.2% of T2-derived neurons.
source: In neurons, we found that cholinergic neurons were most abundant (21%), followed by glutamatergic neurons (12%), GABAergic neurons (9%), tyraminergic neurons (2.6%), dopaminergic neurons (1.2%), serotonergic neurons (1.2%), and octopaminergic neurons (0.7%).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the neurotransmitter expression analysis shown in Figure 3.

claim: Serotonergic neurons comprise 1.2% of T2-derived neurons.
source: In neurons, we found that cholinergic neurons were most abundant (21%), followed by glutamatergic neurons (12%), GABAergic neurons (9%), tyraminergic neurons (2.6%), dopaminergic neurons (1.2%), serotonergic neurons (1.2%), and octopaminergic neurons (0.7%).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the neurotransmitter expression analysis shown in Figure 3.

claim: Octopaminergic neurons comprise 0.7% of T2-derived neurons.
source: In neurons, we found that cholinergic neurons were most abundant (21%), followed by glutamatergic neurons (12%), GABAergic neurons (9%), tyraminergic neurons (2.6%), dopaminergic neurons (1.2%), serotonergic neurons (1.2%), and octopaminergic neurons (0.7%).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the neurotransmitter expression analysis shown in Figure 3.

claim: 12% of T2-derived neurons co-express two or three neurotransmitters.
source: Additionally, 12% of neurons were co-expressing two or three neurotransmitters.
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the neurotransmitter expression analysis shown in Figure 3H.

claim: 40% of neurons in the T2 atlas were not expressing any neurotransmitter with a log normalized expression <2.
source: The remaining 40% in our atlas were not expressing any neurotransmitter with a log normalized expression <2 (Figure 3H); this is similar to the ratios in the adult midbrain (Croset et al., 2018) and optic lobes (Konstantinides et al., 2022).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the neurotransmitter expression analysis shown in Figure 3H, compared to previous studies.

claim: The ratio of neurons not expressing neurotransmitters is similar to the ratios in the adult midbrain and optic lobes.
source: The remaining 40% in our atlas were not expressing any neurotransmitter with a log normalized expression <2 (Figure 3H); this is similar to the ratios in the adult midbrain (Croset et al., 2018) and optic lobes (Konstantinides et al., 2022).
evidence: This is a comparison with previous studies, supported by citations.

claim: The study sub-clustered 12,315 glial nuclei from clusters that expressed the pan glial marker repo in the T2 atlas.
source: We sub-clustered from the T2 atlas for 12,315 glial nuclei from clusters that expressed the pan glial marker repo (Figure 4A; Campbell et al., 1994; Xiong et al., 1994).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the T2 glial analysis shown in Figure 4A, supported by citations.

claim: The T2 glial atlas identified glial cell types: astrocytes, cortex, ensheathing, astrocyte-like, and two surface glial subtypes, perineurial and subperineurial.
source: Similar to our T1+T2 glial atlas, we identified glial cell types: astrocytes, cortex, ensheathing, astrocyte-like, and two surface glial subtypes, perineurial and subperineurial, based on canonical glial makers (Figure 4B; Supplementary file 9).
evidence: This is a finding from the T2 glial analysis shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Some glial subtypes mapped to several subclusters including ensheathing, astrocytes, and chiasm.
source: In line with our T1+T2 atlas and previous glia cell atlas (Lago-Baldaia et al., 2023), some subtypes mapped to several subclusters including ensheathing, astrocytes, and chiasm (Figure 4A–B).
evidence: This is a finding from the T2 glial analysis shown in Figure 4A-B, compared to previous studies.

claim: The study identified chiasm glia that may represent the migratory chiasm glia generated from the DL1 lineage.
source: Interestingly, we identified chiasm glia that may represent the migratory chiasm glia generated from the DL1 lineage (Viktorin et al., 2013; see Discussion).
evidence: This is a finding from the T2 glial analysis, with a citation to support the identity of chiasm glia.

claim: The T2 atlas contains the expected glial cell types.
source: We conclude that our T2 atlas contains the expected glial cell types.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on comparison with known glial cell types.

claim: The T2 glial atlas contained two female enriched clusters: ensheathing/astrocyte (cluster 7) and chiasm (cluster 5).
source: We found that the T2 glial atlas contained two female enriched clusters: ensheathing/astrocyte (cluster 7) and chiasm (cluster 5), and one male enriched cluster: the astrocyte-like (cluster 3; Figure 5B).
evidence: This is a finding from the sex-bias analysis shown in Figure 5B.

claim: The T2 glial atlas contained one male enriched cluster: the astrocyte-like (cluster 3).
source: We found that the T2 glial atlas contained two female enriched clusters: ensheathing/astrocyte (cluster 7) and chiasm (cluster 5), and one male enriched cluster: the astrocyte-like (cluster 3; Figure 5B).
evidence: This is a finding from the sex-bias analysis shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Female glial nuclei expressed higher levels of genes including the female-specific genes yp1, yp2, and yp3.
source: We found female nuclei expressed higher levels of genes including the female-specific genes yp1, yp2, and yp3 (Figure 5C; Warren et al., 1979).
evidence: This is a finding from the differential expression analysis shown in Figure 5C, supported by a citation.

claim: Female glial nuclei were enriched for dsx.
source: Additionally, female nuclei were enriched for dsx (Supplementary file 10).
evidence: This is a finding from the differential expression analysis.

claim: Male glial nuclei expressed higher levels of genes including the male-specific genes lncRNA:rox1/2 and fru.
source: Male glial nuclei expressed higher levels of genes including the male-specific genes lncRNA:rox1/2 and fru (Figure 5C; Supplementary file 10; Amrein and Axel, 1997; Meller et al., 1997; Ryner et al., 1996).
evidence: This is a finding from the differential expression analysis shown in Figure 5C, supported by citations.

claim: Male and female adult T2 glia have sex-specific differences in gene expression within the same glial cell type.
source: We conclude that male and female adult T2 glia have sex-specific differences in gene expression within the same glial cell type.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the differential expression analysis.

claim: The study identified 14 neuronal clusters with disproportionate amounts of male and female nuclei.
source: We identified 14 neuronal clusters with disproportionate amounts of male and female nuclei (Figure 5F).
evidence: This is a finding from the sex-bias analysis shown in Figure 5F.

claim: Female neuronal nuclei expressed higher levels of the female-specific genes yp1, yp2, and yp3.
source: Similar to the T2 glia sex differences, we found female nuclei expressed higher levels of the female-specific genes yp1, yp2, and yp3 (Figure 5G; Warren et al., 1979).
evidence: This is a finding from the differential expression analysis shown in Figure 5G, supported by a citation.

claim: Female neuronal nuclei were enriched for dsx.
source: Additionally, female nuclei were enriched for dsx (Supplementary file 11).
evidence: This is a finding from the differential expression analysis.

claim: Male neuronal nuclei expressed higher levels of the male-specific genes lncRNA:rox1/2 and fru.
source: Male neuronal nuclei expressed higher levels of the male-specific genes lncRNA:rox1/2 and fru (Figure 5G; Supplementary file 11; Amrein and Axel, 1997; Meller et al., 1997; Ryner et al., 1996).
evidence: This is a finding from the differential expression analysis shown in Figure 5G, supported by citations.

claim: Male and female adult T2 neurons have sex-specific differences in gene expression within the same neuronal subtype.
source: We conclude that male and female adult T2 neurons have sex-specific differences in gene expression within the same neuronal subtype.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the differential expression analysis.

claim: The study identified 13 neuropeptides with enriched expression in a limited number of clusters.
source: Among the 49 neuropeptides in Drosophila, we identified 13 with enriched expression in a limited number of clusters, making them suitable as cluster-defining markers (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is a finding from the neuropeptide expression analysis shown in Figure 6A.

claim: All neuropeptide-expressing clusters co-express one or more neurotransmitters.
source: We found that all neuropeptide-expressing clusters, co-express one or more neurotransmitters (see Figure 3H).
evidence: This is a finding from the co-expression analysis shown in Figure 6A and Figure 3H.

claim: Clusters 100 and 128 express NPF and AstA.
source: For example, in some cases, one cluster expresses two or more neuropeptide genes (e.g. clusters 100 and 128 express NPF and AstA); conversely, we also observe one neuropeptide expressed in multiple clusters (e.g. Ms, 2 clusters; Tk, 2 clusters; Figure 6A).
evidence: This is a finding from the neuropeptide expression analysis shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Ms is expressed in 2 clusters.
source: For example, in some cases, one cluster expresses two or more neuropeptide genes (e.g. clusters 100 and 128 express NPF and AstA); conversely, we also observe one neuropeptide expressed in multiple clusters (e.g. Ms, 2 clusters; Tk, 2 clusters; Figure 6A).

claim: Tk is expressed in 2 clusters.
source: For example, in some cases, one cluster expresses two or more neuropeptide genes (e.g. clusters 100 and 128 express NPF and AstA); conversely, we also observe one neuropeptide expressed in multiple clusters (e.g. Ms, 2 clusters; Tk, 2 clusters; Figure 6A).

claim: T2-derived Ms-2A-LexA-expressing neurons project to multiple layers of the dorsal fan-shaped body and the entire ellipsoid body.
source: This method revealed the morphology of specific T2-derived peptidergic neurons. We first assayed Ms+ neurons because Wolff et al., 2025 reported that at least two FB neurons, FB4Z and FB5R express Ms and they target to two distinct FB layers. However, we found that T2-derived Ms-2A-LexA-expressing neurons project to multiple layers of the dorsal fan-shaped body and the entire ellipsoid body, suggesting an unknown class of Ms+ neurons targeting to EB and/or FB (Figure 6C–C'', Video 1).
evidence: This is a finding from the imaging analysis shown in Figure 6C-C'' and Video 1.

claim: Ms is mainly expressed in clusters 157 and 160.
source: In our atlas, Ms is mainly expressed in clusters 157 and 160; however, we cannot distinguish the corresponding identity of each neuron.
evidence: This is a finding from the neuropeptide expression analysis.

claim: NPF-2A-lexA and AstA-2A-lexA label neurons with indistinguishable numbers of cells and projections.
source: We used NPF-2A-lexA and AstA-2A-lexA to label each class of neurons. We found that they were generated at indistinguishable numbers of cells and projections: both had ~20 neurons projecting to a lateral domain of the ellipsoid body and the same two layers of the fan-shaped body (Figure 6D–E; Video 2 and Video 3).
evidence: This is a finding from the imaging analysis shown in Figure 6D-E, Video 2 and Video 3.

claim: Both NPF+ and AstA+ neurons had ~20 neurons projecting to a lateral domain of the ellipsoid body and the same two layers of the fan-shaped body.
source: We used NPF-2A-lexA and AstA-2A-lexA to label each class of neurons. We found that they were generated at indistinguishable numbers of cells and projections: both had ~20 neurons projecting to a lateral domain of the ellipsoid body and the same two layers of the fan-shaped body (Figure 6D–E; Video 2 and Video 3).
evidence: This is a finding from the imaging analysis shown in Figure 6D-E, Video 2 and Video 3.

claim: The study found high correlations of multiple TFs to each neuropeptide.
source: To address this, we performed an unbiased correlation analysis of TF and neuropeptide expression patterns across all cells in our dataset to identify potential regulatory relationships. Interestingly, we found high correlations of multiple TFs to each neuropeptide (Figure 6, Figure 6—figure supplement 1, Supplementary file 12).
evidence: This is a finding from the correlation analysis shown in Figure 6 and Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: Most clusters expressed a unique TF combination.
source: Thus, we assayed each class of TFs to determine how many were expressed in cluster-specific (i.e. neuron-specific) patterns. We found that most clusters expressed a unique TF combination (Figure 7).
evidence: This is a finding from the TF expression analysis shown in Figure 7.

claim: All zinc-finger TFs are expressed in unique combinatorial codes.
source: This is true for all zinc-finger TFs (Figure 7A) and helix-turn-helix TFs (Figure 7B).
evidence: This is a finding from the TF expression analysis shown in Figure 7A.

claim: All helix-turn-helix TFs are expressed in unique combinatorial codes.
source: This is true for all zinc-finger TFs (Figure 7A) and helix-turn-helix TFs (Figure 7B).
evidence: This is a finding from the TF expression analysis shown in Figure 7B.

claim: Nearly all clusters expressed a unique combination of homeodomain TFs.
source: Nearly, all clusters expressed a unique combination of homeodomain TFs (Figure 7C), with only a few clusters sharing a homeodomain code (Figure 7C').
evidence: This is a finding from the TF expression analysis shown in Figure 7C.

claim: Only a few clusters share a homeodomain code.
source: Nearly, all clusters expressed a unique combination of homeodomain TFs (Figure 7C), with only a few clusters sharing a homeodomain code (Figure 7C').
evidence: This is a finding from the TF expression analysis shown in Figure 7C'.

claim: Basic domain, unspecified domain, and high mobility group TFs were more promiscuously expressed.
source: In contrast, basic domain, unspecified domain, and high mobility group TFs were more promiscuously expressed (Figure 7D).
evidence: This is a finding from the TF expression analysis shown in Figure 7D.

claim: Zinc finger, helix-turn-helix, and homeodomain TFs are good candidates for forming unique combinatorial codes that should be tested for a role in generating neuronal diversity.
source: We conclude that zinc finger, helix-turn-helix, and homeodomain TFs are good candidates for forming unique combinatorial codes that should be tested for a role in generating neuronal diversity.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the TF expression patterns observed.

source: Percentage of clusters with unique combinations of TF expression based on TF class zinc finger TFs = 100% (161 unique clusters), helix-turn-helix TFs = 100% (161 unique clusters), homeodomain TFs = 93.8% (150 unique clusters), basic domain TFs = 69.6% (112 unique clusters), unidentified DNA binding domain TFs = 59% (95 unique clusters), high motility group TFs = 34.2% (55 unique clusters).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the TF combinatorial analysis shown in Figure 7.

claim: The T2 atlas can be used to link known neuron subtypes to their transcriptome.
source: We conclude that our T2 atlas can be used to link known neuron subtypes to their transcriptome (Figure 9).
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the mapping results shown in Figure 9.

claim: The T1-derived population contains fewer distinct neuronal clusters (114 clusters) than the T2-derived neuronal population (161 clusters).
source: Interestingly, we observed fewer distinct neuronal clusters in the T1-derived population (114 clusters; Figure 2—figure supplement 1) than in the T2-derived neuronal population (161 clusters; Figure 2).
evidence: This is a comparison of the number of clusters between T1 and T2 atlases.

claim: T1-derived progeny contain a large population of transcriptionally similar Kenyon cells of the MB.
source: This could be due to the T1-derived progeny containing a large population of transcriptionally similar Kenyon cells of the MB, whereas T2-derived clusters contain fewer, but transcriptionally more diverse, cells than T1-derived progeny.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the difference in cluster numbers between T1 and T2 atlases.

claim: T2-derived clusters contain fewer, but transcriptionally more diverse, cells than T1-derived progeny.
source: This could be due to the T1-derived progeny containing a large population of transcriptionally similar Kenyon cells of the MB, whereas T2-derived clusters contain fewer, but transcriptionally more diverse, cells than T1-derived progeny.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the difference in cluster numbers between T1 and T2 atlases.

claim: T2 NBs make distinct neurons across the temporal axis of T2 NBs, plus unique neurons across the INP temporal axis.
source: Our results are consistent with lineage analysis of T2 NBs, which make distinct neurons across the temporal axis of T2 NBs, plus unique neurons across the INP temporal axis (Doe, 2017; Ito et al., 2013; Sullivan et al., 2019; Wang et al., 2014; Yang et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Doe, 2017; Ito et al., 2013; Sullivan et al., 2019; Wang et al., 2014; Yang et al., 2013.

claim: Co-expression of neurotransmitters has been reported in other systems.
source: Co-expression of neurotransmitters has been reported in other systems (Granger et al., 2020; Granger et al., 2023; Lozovaya et al., 2018; Meye et al., 2016; Saunders et al., 2015; Shabel et al., 2014; Spitzer, 2015; Takács et al., 2018) and it may be biologically relevant in the T2-derived neurons.
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to studies in other systems.

claim: Co-expression of neurotransmitters may be biologically relevant in the T2-derived neurons.
source: Co-expression of neurotransmitters has been reported in other systems (Granger et al., 2020; Granger et al., 2023; Lozovaya et al., 2018; Meye et al., 2016; Saunders et al., 2015; Shabel et al., 2014; Spitzer, 2015; Takács et al., 2018) and it may be biologically relevant in the T2-derived neurons.
evidence: This is a speculation based on observations in other systems.

claim: Neuropeptides are profoundly important for a vast array of behaviors.
source: Neuropeptides are profoundly important for a vast array of behaviors (Schoofs et al., 2017), and thus our mapping of neuropeptide expression to distinct neuronal subtypes may facilitate a functional analysis linking neuron identity, neuropeptide expression, and behavior.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Schoofs et al., 2017.

claim: Mapping of neuropeptide expression to distinct neuronal subtypes may facilitate a functional analysis linking neuron identity, neuropeptide expression, and behavior.
source: Neuropeptides are profoundly important for a vast array of behaviors (Schoofs et al., 2017), and thus our mapping of neuropeptide expression to distinct neuronal subtypes may facilitate a functional analysis linking neuron identity, neuropeptide expression, and behavior.
evidence: This is a statement about the potential future utility of the data.

claim: The lack of differential gene expression between T1- and T2-derived glia suggests these cell types are similar despite different developmental origins.
source: The lack of differential gene expression between T1- and T2-derived glia suggests these cell types are similar despite different developmental origins.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the differential expression results.

claim: Chiasm glia have been shown to be derived from the T2 lineage DL1 and migrate into the optic lobe.
source: Additionally, we captured chiasm glia that have been shown to be derived from the T2 lineage DL1 and migrate into the optic lobe (Viktorin et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Viktorin et al., 2013.

claim: Chiasm glia nuclei could represent either chiasm glia that did not migrate out of the central brain or optic lobe tissue that was not completely removed during dissections.
source: These nuclei could represent either chiasm glia that did not migrate out of the central brain or optic lobe tissue that was not completely removed during dissections.
evidence: This is a speculation about the origin of chiasm glia in the dataset.

claim: The TF combinations may determine neuronal functional properties, by establishing and maintaining neuronal identities.
source: Our atlas showed zinc finger TFs and homeodomain TFs as forming combinatorial codes specific for distinct cell types. This raises the possibility that these TF combinations determine neuronal functional properties, by establishing and maintaining neuronal identities.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the observed TF expression patterns.

claim: TF combinatorial codes determining neuronal identities is consistent with data from C. elegans, mammalian spinal cord, Drosophila optic lobe, leg motor neurons, and VNC.
source: This is consistent with data from C. elegans (Hobert, 2021; Reilly et al., 2020), mammalian spinal cord (Briscoe et al., 2000; Sagner et al., 2021), Drosophila optic lobe (Holguera and Desplan, 2018; Konstantinides et al., 2018), leg motor neurons (Baek et al., 2013; Enriquez et al., 2015), and VNC (Soffers et al., 2024).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to studies in various systems.

claim: The current sparse TF expression patterns may be due, in part, to false negative results due to low read depths.
source: It is also possible that the current sparse TF expression patterns are due, in part, to false negative results due to low read depths.
evidence: This is a speculation about potential technical limitations.
